message.content: Assuming the detonator is being placed on the table during a negotiation, it would be a clever move in principle, but it is not strongly in character for Hux unless the story makes him more desperate and dependent on outside help. Hux’s natural approach is blunt military authority, intimidation, and political posturing, not subtle engineering or gadget work. A disguised thermal detonator would be a nice tactical trick, but it sounds more like something a field operative, droid, or technician would devise than something Hux would personally conceive or build. If the Knights of Ren turned against the First Order as a third party, Hux would likely treat them as dangerous traitors or unstable cultists rather than as a sophisticated enemy worth outwitting. He would probably try to use his rank, stormtrooper support, propaganda, or Kylo Ren’s loyalty to remove them. His character is not that of a patient spy or schemer; he is a bully in a military uniform. So a hidden detonator would be out of step with how he normally operates, especially if he expects the Knights to back down because he is a First Order general. The trick could still be made in character if Hux is cornered, losing control of the situation, and is willing to use an ugly, desperate gambit instead of facing execution or disgrace. In that version, Hux would not be the one crafting the fake holocron. He would have a droid, engineer, or captured prisoner rig it, or he would seize a preexisting device and present it as a relic. The move would fit him as a last-ditch attempt to regain power: bluff, betray, and explode before the Knights can take him down. As a story beat, the idea works best as a risky bluff rather than a guaranteed clever victory. If Hux places the fake holocron on the table as a bargaining chip, intelligence prize, or ceremonial object, it could distract the Knights long enough to trigger it. But the Knights of Ren are battle-hardened, and Ren is Force-sensitive, so they might sense that the object is not what it claims to be or inspect it too closely. That makes the scheme clever, but also fragile, which is good for tension.
